title: Italy and Byzantium
hook: Jews have lived in Rome since before the Temple fell

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Karaites: a movement that set the oral law aside, and the rabbis who argued back. Your line was argument sharpens. Did a disagreement sharpen something in you? Today we leave Babylon and head west, to a very old address. Day nine hundred seventeen.

In the Roman Forum stands a stone arch built for a general named Titus. Walk under it and look up at the inside wall. Carved soldiers are carrying a great lampstand on poles, the Temple menorah, out of a city they have just burned. It is a victory picture, made by the winners. Some Roman Jews keep a custom of not walking under that arch at all. And here is the strange part. Their community was in Rome before the arch went up, and it is still there now that the empire that built it is gone. Today, the old Jewish communities of Italy and Byzantium: people who stayed, generation after generation, in the same streets.
screen: `AN ARCH FOR TITUS.` → `A MENORAH CARRIED AWAY.` → `THE COMMUNITY THAT STAYED.`

segments.voice: Start with the oldest written traces. The first book of Maccabees tells how Judah Maccabee sent envoys to Rome to make a treaty of friendship. That is a story from before the Temple fell, and tradition in Rome's Jewish community points back to ties like it. Then the New Testament gives two small snapshots. The book of Acts mentions a couple who had to leave the city, in the King James words, "because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome." And later, when Paul reaches Rome, Acts says he "called the chief of the Jews together." So by then there were Jewish leaders in the city to call. Even in stories about someone else, a Jewish community is already living there. Now turn east. When the Roman Empire split, its eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, is what historians call Byzantium. Greek-speaking Jews lived across its towns, in Greece, in the islands, in southern Italy, which Byzantium ruled for a long stretch. Their descendants are sometimes called Romaniote Jews, and they kept their own prayer customs and poems. From southern Italy comes a family chronicle in Hebrew, the Scroll of Ahimaaz, where a writer traces his ancestors through generations of teachers, poets and community leaders, with miracle stories woven in. History and family memory in one scroll. Life under Byzantine rule was not easy. The same scroll remembers an emperor who pressed Jews to convert, and times of hardship. But the communities held. And here is the thread that matters for tomorrow: teachers and families from Italy carried learning north, over the Alps. An old community is not just old. It is a place that keeps handing things on.
screen: `ENVOYS TO ROME.` · then, large: `CALLED THE CHIEF OF THE JEWS TOGETHER.` · `GREEK-SPEAKING JEWS IN BYZANTIUM.` · `A FAMILY SCROLL THAT HANDS THINGS ON.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: think about the oldest community near you. It might be a synagogue, a church, a mosque, a temple, a social club, a family farm, a neighborhood that has kept its name. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring that place to mind. Who were the first people to gather there? What did they carry with them, a language, a recipe, a song? What has it outlasted? Later today, if you have a minute, look up one fact about it. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for the people who stayed. The bell holds the time.
Italy and Byzantium. Jews in Rome before the arch was built, and Greek-speaking Jews across the eastern empire, keeping their own customs. Today's word.
Your line: old communities. Today, ask one older person how long their family or group has been where it is, and listen to the whole answer. Day nine hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Roman Jews and Romaniote Jews keep their own synagogue customs and prayer traditions, distinct from both Ashkenazi and Sephardi rites, and some still gather in historic synagogues in Rome and in Greece.

fork.setup: you are a Jewish leader in Rome. the emperor Claudius has ordered Jews out of the city. what does Acts show happened next?
options: Jews never lived in Rome again.
a Jewish couple left, and later Paul found Jewish leaders in Rome.
everyone moved to Babylon for good.
fork.reveal: Acts mentions a couple who left because of Claudius, yet later Paul calls the chief of the Jews together in Rome. The community was there again.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jewish history in Europe begins in Germany or Spain.
what it means: Jews lived in Rome and across the Greek-speaking east long before, and kept their own customs.
what a scholar hears: Acts already places Jewish leaders in Rome, and the Hebrew Scroll of Ahimaaz traces a southern Italian family through generations.

notes: Claims rule: the outline hook 'Jews have lived in Rome since before the Temple fell' is framed through 1 Maccabees 8 (envoys to Rome) and Roman Jewish tradition; no dates or counts are given.
The custom of not walking under the Arch of Titus is described as something 'some Roman Jews' keep; please confirm wording.
Romaniote: 'from the Greek word for Roman' is a naming claim; please confirm or cut.
Byzantine rule over southern Italy and periods of pressure to convert are stated without dates or emperors' names; please confirm framing.
The Scroll of Ahimaaz described as a Hebrew family chronicle with miracle stories; please confirm.
The claim that teachers and families from Italy carried learning north sets up tomorrow (tradition of the Kalonymus family); please confirm.
The Apocrypha (1 Maccabees) and Acts are used as historical witnesses, not as Jewish scripture; a Keeper may want that made explicit.
